transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I feel like my mind is constantly spinning about work and I just can’t shut the worrying off, no matter what I’m doing. It’s gotten to the point where it feels completely overwhelming, and I realized I need some help trying to manage it.
Did this anxiety start after a specific stressful event or major life change, or has it been more of an ongoing pattern? About how long has it been going on?

It really started about 14 months ago when I was promoted to lead a larger regional sales team with very aggressive quarterly targets. Since then, it has turned into a constant, daily pattern of worrying that I just can't shake. It's been going on steadily like this for a little over a year now.

Besides work, do you also find yourself worrying a lot about other parts of life, like your health, family, finances, or everyday responsibilities? Or is the anxiety mainly limited to your job and sales targets?

While work and sales are the main triggers, the anxiety definitely spreads into other areas of my life. For instance, I constantly worry about our finances, like how my husband and I would pay the mortgage if my commissions drop. It’s so persistent that it keeps me from enjoying everyday moments, even just trying to relax and watch a show with my husband.

Along with the constant worrying, have you also had symptoms like feeling restless or on edge, getting tired easily, trouble concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, or problems sleeping? If so, which ones have been happening most days?

Yes, I've definitely been struggling with several of those, especially sleep issues where I lie awake for hours replaying work conversations or wake up at 3 AM with my mind already racing. During the day, I feel constantly revved up and restless, like I've had too much coffee and just can't sit still. I've also been incredibly irritable lately, snapping at my husband and teammates over minor things, which makes me feel terrible.

How much is this anxiety affecting your day-to-day functioning—for example, your work performance, relationships, or ability to handle routine tasks? Have you been avoiding anything or missing work because of it?

It's affecting my life a lot; my performance reviews have actually slipped, and my manager recently warned me that I seem scattered in meetings. I've also pulled back from my cycling club and theatre group, canceling plans at the last minute so much that people have mostly stopped inviting me. I've just been staying home to work or worry instead of doing the things I used to love.

Have you been using a lot of caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol, cannabis, or any medications or drugs that seem to make the anxiety worse? Do you have any medical problems like thyroid issues or heart symptoms that started around the same time?

No, I don't use recreational drugs or cannabis, and I only drink alcohol occasionally. The feeling of having too much coffee is just how my body physically feels restless and tense, not from actually drinking a lot of caffeine. I also don't have any medical conditions like thyroid or heart issues.

Do you ever get sudden surges of intense fear or physical symptoms—like your heart racing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, dizziness, or feeling like you might lose control—that peak within minutes? Or is the anxiety more of a steady, ongoing worry throughout the day?

It’s definitely more of a steady, ongoing worry that persists throughout the day rather than sudden surges of panic. While I feel constantly revved up and have a running spreadsheet of worries in my head, I don't experience those sudden, overwhelming attacks with chest tightness or shortness of breath.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes excessive, difficult-to-control worry occurring daily for over a year across multiple domains (work and finances), accompanied by restlessness, irritability, and significant insomnia, with clear functional impairment in work and social life. Anxiety is persistent rather than episodic, and panic attacks, substance-related causes, and relevant medical causes were denied, supporting generalized anxiety disorder.
